answers.answer: No. SCOPe does not support merging these three groups into one homologous superfamily. It unites them only at the fold level, as fold f.21 "Heme-binding four-helical bundle" in class f (membrane and cell surface proteins and peptides), whose fold description is essentially "core: 4 helices, bundle; heme bound between the helices". In SCOP/SCOPe (1.75 through 2.08) that fold is split into two separate superfamilies: f.21.1 "Fumarate reductase respiratory complex transmembrane subunits" (the membrane-anchor subunits of fumarate reductase and succinate:quinone oxidoreductase, e.g. Wolinella succinogenes FrdC from 1qla, E. coli FrdC/FrdD from 1l0v, E. coli SdhC/SdhD from 1nek) and f.21.2 "Transmembrane di-heme cytochromes". The respiratory nitrate reductase gamma chain (E. coli NarI, from 1q16/1y4z) is not a third superfamily: SCOPe places it as a family inside f.21.2, alongside the cytochrome b subunits of the bc1 and b6f complexes and the formate dehydrogenase-N cytochrome b subunit (FdnI, 1kqf chain C). So the evolutionary claims SCOPe makes are asymmetric: (1) di-heme cytochromes and NarI are asserted to be homologous (same superfamily, f.21.2, and NarI/FdnI-type cytochromes are further grouped at family level where sequence similarity is clear); (2) the fumarate reductase/SQR anchor subunits share only the fold (f.21) with them, which in SCOP semantics means a similar topology and heme-packing architecture without evidence of common ancestry. A fold-level match in class f is a particularly weak homology signal because a four-helix transmembrane bundle with hemes ligated by histidines on neighbouring helices is a simple, convergently accessible architecture, and the f.21.1 members themselves vary in heme content (two hemes in W. succinogenes FrdC, one in E. coli SQR, none in E. coli QFR), so the "heme-binding" descriptor is not even uniform within the superfamily. Practical limits: do not transfer function (quinone-site location, electron-transfer direction, heme stoichiometry, interaction with the soluble catalytic subunits) between f.21.1 and f.21.2 members on the basis of SCOPe; do not use a bc1 cytochrome b, NarI or FdnI structure as a homology-modelling template for an SQR/QFR anchor subunit, or vice versa, since fold-only relationships give no reliable residue-level alignment; and do not pick one representative for the whole fold when the intent is to represent a homologous set, because superfamily f.21.1 and f.21.2 need separate representatives (and ASTRAL representative sets are selected within sequence-identity-clustered domains, not across fold-level groups). To argue for a single superfamily one would need evidence SCOPe does not provide: statistically significant sequence or profile-HMM relationships (e.g. shared Pfam clan membership or HHpred hits between the Frd/Sdh anchor families and the NarI/FdnI/cytochrome b families), structure-based alignments showing conserved positions of the heme-ligating histidines beyond what the bundle geometry forces, conserved gene-neighbourhood/operon context linking the two groups, or a curated homology call from an independent classification such as ECOD or CATH that explicitly groups them. Absent that, the correct SCOPe statement is: same fold (f.21), two superfamilies (f.21.1 vs f.21.2), with the nitrate reductase gamma chain belonging to the di-heme cytochrome superfamily rather than to the fumarate reductase one.
